name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
One of my earlier experiences I still remember is when my grandfather bought a completely broken-down 1955 Caterpillar D6 bulldozer for five thousand dollars, even though a new one would have cost more than a hundred thousand. We spent the whole summer fixing it, just the two of us out on the ranch.

We'd order parts by mail, including big transmission gears and so on, and they'd show up too heavy to lift by hand. So we'd build a crane, right there, because the nearest place to rent equipment was an hour away and my grandfather just didn't really believe in calling somebody.

He made his own veterinary tools too. I watched him take a piece of wire, heat it up, pound it thin, drill a hole in it, sharpen it, and that was a suture needle.

I don't think I understood, at the time, that I was being taught anything. It was just a summer. But that's where it came from, this idea that most things are solvable with enough persistence and a little ingenuity, and that waiting around for someone else to fix it is usually just the slower, more expensive version of fixing it yourself.

I still think about that experience, especially as a guy who spends most of his time on rockets now.

name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
New Glenn blew up on the pad back in May. We lost the lightning tower, the transporter-erector, and a good portion of the launch infrastructure at LC-36. By some estimates, it was one of the more powerful rocket explosions since the Soviets lost the N1.

And now we’re going with a completely different launch concept instead - a hybrid approach we had already been quietly developing for a later version of the vehicle. It uses existing infrastructure and avoids rebuilding a transporter-erector whose failure mode, well, we now understand a little too well.

Here’s how I think about a decision like that. Most decisions are two-way doors. You walk through, it doesn’t work, you walk back and choose another path. This isn’t really that. How we rebuild this particular piece of infrastructure is close to a one-way door, because whatever we choose now, we’ll be living with it for years of launches. It is the kind of decision you slow down for. Even, perhaps especially, when the whole internet is asking why you haven’t launched yet.

Manufacturing at rate, rebuilding a pad properly - none of that is glamorous. But it is the actual work.

We’ll fly this year. And the pad we fly from will be better than the one we lost.

name: Jeff Bezos
role: Founder, Amazon | Founder, Blue Origin | Executive Chairman
body:
I was at Princeton, majoring in physics with plans to become a theoretical physicist, treating computer science as more of a side hobby I enjoyed. One night my friend Joe and I spent three hours stuck on a tough partial differential equations problem and got nowhere. At the same moment, we both looked up and thought of the same person: a classmate named Yosanta, from Sri Lanka, one of the most brilliant and humble people I'd ever met.

We went to Yosanta's dorm room, showed him the problem, and he stared at it for maybe ten seconds before simply saying "cosine" - that was the answer. I didn't believe him at first, so he wrote out three pages of equations proving it, and everything canceled out perfectly, landing on cosine. When I asked if he'd done it in his head, he said no, he'd solved a similar problem a few years earlier and could map this one onto it, which made the answer immediately obvious.

That moment convinced me that being a theoretical physicist wasn't my path. That field requires a very specific kind of brain-wiring that only a small percentage of people have, unlike other fields where being very good is enough to move the state of the art forward. So I switched to computer science, and that worked out pretty well for me.

It ties into my inventive, lateral-thinking style... coming up with a hundred atypical ideas knowing 99 will fail but one might stick. It shows up in a different domain than math. There are a thousand ways to be smart, and Yosanta's kind of smart just wasn't mine.

When you do the things that come naturally to you, that feel like play, you build specific knowledge no one can train someone else to replace. And you find your cosine.
